messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
parts:
For the ensemble sampler, I'm still unsure of how we want to treat the end results of each walker. For instance, what should bin/print show? Do we want to print each walker out by itself? Or should we just take the best one? Or just the average of the walkers?

As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of the methods to take in a vector of samples instead of just a sample. Then, for metropolis, RM-HMC, NUTS the vector will be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.


Peter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
parts:
On 5/23/13 3:30 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> For the ensemble sampler, I'm still unsure of how we want to treat the end results of each walker. For instance, what
> should bin/print show? Do we want to print each walker out by itself? Or should we just take the best one? Or just the
> average of the walkers?

bin/print consolidates multiple chains into a single output
and we want to treat each walker as an individual chain.

We can't average them or just get the posterior mean. The
whole point of MCMC is to get samples representing the posterior
(co-)variation.

We can't take the "best" one because (a) we have no way to know
which is best, and (b) even if we did, it probably wouldn't satisfy
detailed balance.

> As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of
> the methods to take in a vector of samples instead of just a sample. Then, for metropolis, RM-HMC, NUTS the vector will
> be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes
> in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.

The impact on command is one of the reasons I think it's important
to think about this sooner rather than later.

For design, always work backwards from what we want out.

For the walker setup, we essentially want to treat each walker
as its own chain. That means we shouldn't have to modify bin/print
at all, and hopefully won't have to modify RStan much.

Andrew wants to run multiple instances of these
ensemble methods, too. But that should also be OK -- just more
chains to go in the mix.

So to get the output we need, it suffices to have walker n
in ensemble m write to its own samples_M_N.csv file.

Then we just need the input config. That's going to have to vary
for each class of samplers. Here, the issue is that we need to
initialize each walker in each ensemble. In RStan, we can provide
an initialization function, so it can be run multiple times and perhaps
have some randomness in it. We haven't done anything like that for
command-line Stan, so it'd be OK for now to only allow random initialization
for the ensembles. (Eventually I'd like to get an initialization
value and then add some noise around it --- that is, recenter the
init=0 at a given value.)

The rest of the changes are going to be internal state. This you
are certainly going to have to do differently for the ensembles. But
that doesn't mean you have to do it by generalizing what we already have.
You can write a new base class for ensemble samplers and use that.
You can reuse the sample class for a single position of a single walker.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
parts:
I spent some time this weekend thinking about ensemble samplers, and I think the most general way to approach them is via Neal's ensemble state methods.  That is, we consider mappings between single states and ensembles that preserve detailed balance.  The only difficulty is that we're not mapping from (single state -> ensemble -> single state), but rather (many states -> ensemble -> many states) the mappings aren't hard to manipulate (basically a uniform distribution on the permutation group will do) but I'm not sure if there are any issues with using multiple states while preserving a true Markov chain.

In any case, the encapsulation I was considering would be of the form

class ensemble_sampler: public sampler {

public:

  vector<sampler> samplers;

  transition() {
    for (sampler in samplers) sampler.transition()
  }

  write_state() {
   random_permute(samplers)
    for (sampler in samplers) sampler.write_state()
  }

}

We'd have to tweak our flow a bit (transition would have to use the internal state of sampler and not a given sample, mcmc_writer would have to be tweaked slightly) but then we'd be able to add any ensemble method (including multiple chains) without changing command.hpp.

My main concern is that the user isn't going to know what to do with a bunch of output files.  But if we give them a single output file then they can go about their business without any trouble.

As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of

be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes
in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.
